cards.front: Is there a limit to how long a Java identifier may be?
cards.extra: The JLS defines an identifier as an unlimited-length sequence of Java letters and Java digits whose first character must be a Java letter. Nothing in the compiler truncates or penalises a long name, so readability is the only real limit.

cards.front: Which characters may follow the first character of a Java identifier?
cards.back: Any Java letter or Java digit — digits are allowed from the second position on
cards.extra: IdentifierChars is one Java letter followed by zero or more Java letters-or-digits, so i3, MAX_VALUE and x2 are legal. A digit in position one is still an error, which is why 1stPlace does not compile.

cards.front: Which two ASCII symbols count as Java letters for historical reasons?
cards.back: The dollar sign $ and the underscore _
cards.extra: The Java letters are A–Z, a–z, plus $ (U+0024) and _ (U+005F), admitted only for historical reasons. Every other Java letter comes from Unicode, not from ASCII punctuation.

cards.front: When should a dollar sign appear in a Java identifier?
cards.back: Only in mechanically generated source, or to reach legacy names
cards.extra: The JLS says the dollar sign should be used only in mechanically generated source code or, rarely, to access pre-existing names on legacy systems. It compiles wherever a letter does, so this is a style rule that no compiler enforces.

cards.front: Why can a single underscore _ no longer name a variable?
cards.back: Because _ is a reserved keyword since Java 9
cards.extra: The JLS lists _ among the reserved keywords, and it may appear in identifiers of two or more characters but not as a one-character identifier. Java 8 still accepted a lone underscore, so old code stops compiling on upgrade.

cards.front: May an identifier be spelled like a keyword, or like true, false or null?
cards.back: No — tokenization makes them a keyword or literal, and that is a compile error
cards.extra: An identifier is IdentifierChars but not a ReservedKeyword, BooleanLiteral or NullLiteral, and the check happens during tokenization. So int class = 1; and int null = 1; both fail before any type checking begins.

cards.front: May an identifier be spelled like a contextual keyword such as var?
cards.back: Yes in ordinary positions — the token stays an identifier where the grammar does not expect the keyword
cards.extra: Contextual keywords are reduced to keywords only in the constructs that use them, so var works as a field or parameter name. As a type name it fails, because there the sequence must be a TypeIdentifier.

cards.front: Are two identifiers that look identical when rendered necessarily the same?
cards.back: No — every code point must match
cards.extra: Latin A, Greek Α and Cyrillic а render alike but are three identifiers. The JLS states plainly that identifiers with the same external appearance may yet be different, so a homoglyph typo compiles as a brand-new name.

cards.front: Is Á typed as one character the same identifier as A followed by a combining accent?
cards.back: No — composed and decomposed forms are different identifiers
cards.extra: The JLS treats a precomposed LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A ACUTE as different from A followed by NON-SPACING ACUTE. A name pasted from another editor in a different normalisation form therefore fails to match the declaration, even though it looks identical.

cards.front: Which methods does the JLS defer to for the definition of a Java letter?
cards.extra: Instead of listing characters, the JLS makes a Java letter whatever isJavaIdentifierStart accepts, and a Java letter-or-digit whatever isJavaIdentifierPart accepts. isJavaIdentifierStart is true for letters, letter numbers and currency symbols, which is why € may begin an identifier.

cards.front: Can a Java identifier be written in Chinese, Greek or Cyrillic letters?
cards.back: Yes — any Unicode Java letter is accepted
cards.extra: Letters and digits may be drawn from the entire Unicode character set, so identifiers can be written in the programmer's native language. 変数 and μέτρηση both compile; only the ASCII convention keeps most production code Latin.
